question: Which delivery semantic never loses messages but may process some more than once?
options: At-most-once
At-least-once
Exactly-once
Best-effort-once
explanation: At-least-once (commit offsets after processing, with retries) never loses data but can reprocess records on failure, producing duplicates. At-most-once may lose data but never duplicates.

question: How does consumer offset-commit timing determine the delivery guarantee?
options: Committing before processing gives at-least-once; committing after gives at-most-once
Committing before processing gives at-most-once (may lose); committing after successful processing gives at-least-once (may duplicate)
Offset-commit timing has no effect on the guarantee
Only automatic commits can produce at-least-once semantics
explanation: Committing the offset before processing means a crash skips the record (at-most-once, possible loss); committing only after processing succeeds means a crash reprocesses it (at-least-once, possible duplicate).

question: What kind of duplicates does enable.idempotence on the producer actually remove?
options: Duplicates from consumer reprocessing after a crash
Duplicates from producer retries within a single producer session
All possible duplicates end-to-end across the pipeline
Duplicates caused by consumer group rebalances
explanation: The idempotent producer uses a producer ID and per-partition sequence numbers so the broker discards duplicate retried appends. It does NOT address consumer-reprocessing duplicates under at-least-once.

question: What is the pragmatic pattern most data pipelines use to achieve an exactly-once end state without Kafka transactions?
options: At-most-once delivery with acks=0
At-least-once delivery plus an idempotent sink (keyed upsert or event-id dedup)
Committing offsets before processing every record
Disabling retries on the producer entirely
explanation: At-least-once delivery combined with an idempotent sink (e.g., INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE keyed on a business/event id) absorbs reprocessing duplicates so the final table reflects each event once, with no transaction coordinator needed.

question: Why can leaving enable.auto.commit=true (the default) make the delivery guarantee hard to reason about?
options: It permanently disables offset tracking
It commits offsets on a timer independent of whether processing succeeded, giving a fuzzy at-least-once with an ill-defined crash boundary
It automatically enables exactly-once semantics
It forces every consumer into at-most-once mode
explanation: Auto-commit advances offsets on a timer (auto.commit.interval.ms) regardless of processing progress, so the effective guarantee is a loose at-least-once with an unpredictable failure boundary. Disable it and commit explicitly for precise semantics.
